content: Orthostatic hypotension, also known as postural hypotension, is defined as a decrease in systolic blood pressure of at least 20 mmHg or a decrease in diastolic blood pressure of at least 10 mmHg within three minutes of standing. A similar drop in blood pressure during a head-up tilt test at 60 degrees also qualifies as orthostatic hypotension. This condition can be asymptomatic or present with symptoms such as lightheadedness, dizziness, blurred vision, or cognitive impairment. It can have acute or chronic causes, and its management can be particularly challenging in patients who also experience supine hypertension. Classification of Orthostatic Hypotension: 1. Initial Orthostatic Hypotension (iOH): This is most commonly observed in healthy adolescents. It is characterized by a brief drop in blood pressure of >40 mmHg systolic or >20 mmHg diastolic, accompanied by symptoms of cerebral hypoperfusion (e.g., dizziness or lightheadedness) within 5 to 15 seconds of standing. Symptoms typically resolve within 20 seconds. 2. Neurogenic Orthostatic Hypotension (nOH): This occurs due to a failure of sympathetic noradrenergic nerves to initiate the reflexive cardiovascular responses necessary to maintain blood pressure during orthostatic stress. It is defined as a sustained drop in blood pressure of >20 mmHg systolic or >10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes of standing or head-up tilt, with or without symptoms. 3. Delayed Orthostatic Hypotension (dOH): This is defined as a drop in blood pressure meeting the criteria for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension but occurring after three minutes of standing. 4. Neurally Mediated Syncope (vOH): Also referred to as vasodepressor or vasovagal syncope, this involves a sudden withdrawal of sympathetic vasopressor tone, often during prolonged standing, in patients with an otherwise intact autonomic nervous system. 5. Cardiovascular Orthostatic Hypotension (cOH): This results from intravascular hypovolemia or reduced cardiac output, often accompanied by compensatory tachycardia. 6. Orthostatic Pseudohypotension (pOH): This refers to an apparent drop in blood pressure due to elevated baseline supine blood pressure, which may be caused by insufficient rest before measurement, recumbent hypertension, or labile hypertension. Pathophysiology: When standing, approximately 500 to 1000 mL of blood pools in the lower extremities and splanchnic circulation, leading to a rapid reduction in venous return to the heart. This decreases ventricular filling pressures, cardiac output, and systemic blood pressure. Baroreceptors, primarily located in the aorta and carotid arteries, detect these changes and respond by increasing sympathetic outflow and decreasing parasympathetic activity. This results in arteriolar and venous vasoconstriction, which helps restore venous return and cardiac output, thereby limiting the drop in blood pressure. This compensatory mechanism is known as the baroreflex. Dysfunction of the baroreflex, volume depletion, or adverse effects of certain medications can impair this response, leading to orthostatic hypotension and symptoms of cerebral hypoperfusion, such as dizziness, nausea, headache, blurred vision, and cognitive impairment. Causes: Common causes of orthostatic hypotension include: Autonomic neuropathies (e.g., Parkinson’s disease, diabetes) Volume depletion (e.g., due to vomiting, diarrhea, or hemorrhage) Prolonged bed rest Certain medications (e.g., antihypertensives) Differentiation from Other Conditions: Orthostatic hypotension must be distinguished from other conditions such as neurogenic syncope, cardiogenic syncope, situational syncope, postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), and vasovagal syncope. Epidemiology: The incidence of orthostatic hypotension-related hospitalizations is approximately 36 per 100,000 adults, increasing to 233 per 100,000 in individuals over 75 years of age. Its prevalence rises with age, affecting about 5% of individuals under 50 years old and up to 20% of those over 65 years old. It affects men and women equally. Risk Factors: Risk factors for developing orthostatic hypotension include: Age >65 years Use of certain medications Autonomic neuropathies Volume depletion Postpartum period Prolonged bed rest Diagnosis: Orthostatic hypotension is diagnosed by measuring blood pressure and heart rate in both supine and standing positions. A drop of at least 20 mmHg in systolic blood pressure or 10 mmHg in diastolic blood pressure within 2-5 minutes of standing confirms the diagnosis. The absence of a normal rise in heart rate upon standing may indicate autonomic dysfunction. Symptoms: Symptoms of orthostatic hypotension are due to cerebral hypoperfusion and include: Lightheadedness and dizziness upon standing (most common) Generalized weakness Headache Blurred or dimmed vision (sometimes to the point of momentary blindness) Fatigue Cognitive impairment Syncope (in severe cases) Management: Management of orthostatic hypotension focuses on alleviating symptoms, preventing falls, and addressing underlying causes. Treatment can be divided into lifestyle modifications and medical therapy. Non-Pharmacological Therapy: Educating patients about the condition and its triggers. Discontinuing medications that may exacerbate orthostatic hypotension. Avoiding factors such as heat and alcohol that worsen symptoms. Consuming smaller, more frequent meals to prevent postprandial hypotension. Using physical counter-maneuvers, such as contracting lower abdominal muscles while standing. Pharmacological Therapy: First-line medications: Midodrine: Initiated at 2.5 mg to 10 mg three times daily, with a maximum dose of 40 mg/day. Droxidopa: Started at 100 mg and titrated up to 600 mg three times daily. Patients should avoid taking droxidopa within 4-5 hours of bedtime to prevent supine hypertension. Second-line medications: Erythropoietin: Administered subcutaneously or intravenously at doses of 25-75 units/kg three times weekly. Pyridostigmine: Initiated at 30 mg three times daily, up to a maximum of 90 mg three times daily. Caffeine (100-250 mg three times daily with meals). Fludrocortisone or sympathomimetic agents as adjuncts. Prognosis: The prognosis of orthostatic hypotension depends on its underlying cause. While asymptomatic cases may not require treatment, symptomatic cases can lead to complications such as falls, cardiovascular events, cognitive decline, and reduced quality of life. Prevention: Primary prevention strategies include: Wearing an abdominal binder when out of bed. Drinking two 8-ounce glasses of cold water before prolonged standing. Sleeping with the head of the bed elevated. Performing counter-maneuvers, such as contracting lower abdominal muscles while standing. Avoiding triggers such as heat, alcohol, and large meals. By addressing these factors, the risk of orthostatic hypotension and its associated complications can be minimized.
